FIELD NOTE · 02 / 07ABOUT
STOP 02 · ABOUT ME

The Field Camp

⌖ About · The story behind the science

✦

I'm a geoscientist and Ph.D. researcher at the University of Pittsburgh. My work asks what people leave behind in the landscape (metals in sediment, salt in soil, mines under hillsides) and how those legacies change water quality and slope stability.

I combine field investigation, laboratory geochemistry and computational modeling. That means coring ponds and sampling estuaries, running XRD and ICP-OES in the lab, then building Python workflows, Monte Carlo models and machine-learning tools that make the results useful for hazard assessment, infrastructure management and environmental decisions.

Before graduate school I mapped an electricity network as a GIS mapper in Benin City. Since then I've worked with scientists in El Salvador, a Critical Zone team in Texas and transportation agencies in Pennsylvania, and mentored undergraduate researchers along the way.

The Six Outcrops

Each project pairs fieldwork with lab and computational analysis. The impact line is the one-sentence answer.

OUTCROP 01ROAD SALT
Pittsburgh · 2021 to present

Road Salt, Clay Mineralogy and Hillslope Stability

How chloride-rich road salt changes the mineralogy, pore-water chemistry and strength of landslide-prone soils and mudstones across Southwestern Pennsylvania, plus Monte Carlo models of legacy lead that travels with landslides.

  • Impact: road-salt infiltration weakens clay-rich slopes and can remobilize legacy contaminants, informing landslide-risk assessment and infrastructure management.
  • Presented at AGU (2022), the Pennsylvania Transportation Forum (2023) and EEGS (2026).
Quantitative XRDGeotechnical testingMonte Carlo
OUTCROP 02LEGACY METALS
Pittsburgh · Catfish Pond

Legacy Trace Metals in Catfish Pond

Dated sediment cores reconstruct the history of trace-metal contamination. Mixing models and elemental ratios separate the contributions of bedrock, steel slag and industrial soils linked to the Clairton Coke Works.

  • Impact: metal loading kept rising despite emissions controls, because legacy contaminated material is being remobilized. The finding informs watershed management.
Sediment coresMixing modelsSource apportionment
OUTCROP 03RECURRING SLIDES
Southwestern Pennsylvania

Recurring Landslides over Old Mines

Working with geologists, geomorphologists and transportation agencies, this project combines more than 15,000 mapped landslides with geologic maps, mining records and topography to find out why some slopes fail again and again.

  • Impact: quantified how legacy underground mining and bedrock geology combine to drive recurrence, improving regional susceptibility assessment for transportation and land-use planning.
15,000+ landslidesMining recordsGeospatial statistics
OUTCROP 04INVENTORY
IRISE team · Southwestern Pennsylvania

Regional Landslide Inventory and Soil Tools

Part of the IRISE team building a regional landslide inventory for hazard and risk assessment. Led the extraction and analysis of USDA SSURGO soil data and wrote the Python modules that automate it.

  • Impact: a regional landslide inventory and reusable Python tools for SSURGO extraction that speed up regional hazard analyses.
PythonSSURGOSusceptibility
OUTCROP 05RADON
First-author paper · 2024

Rock Fractures and Radon Transport

Characterized fracture networks and their geometry to support fractal modeling of how radon gas migrates through rock.

  • Impact: linked fracture-network geometry to radon migration pathways, published in the Journal of Environmental Radioactivity (2024).
Fracture networksFractal modelingSubsurface gas
OUTCROP 06ESTUARY
Ohio University · 2017 to 2019

Arsenic and Heavy Metals, Barra de Santiago

Designed the study and sampling strategy with scientists from El Salvador and the United States, then mapped arsenic and heavy metals in estuarine sediments and traced their likely sources.

  • Impact: identified unexpected nickel contamination. Published in Water, Air, & Soil Pollution (2025) and presented as an invited talk at CENSALUD, El Salvador.
Estuarine sedimentsArsenicInternational fieldwork
